extracted.intended_audience: criminalists / examining justices / legal investigators / trial judges
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating witness testimony and criminal behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for criminal investigators and judges on how to assess testimony, human behavior, and causal explanations (habit, heredity, prejudice, imitation, passion, honor, superstition) during inquiry and trial. Emphasizes detection of biases, limits of inferences, and signs to test or corroborate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish habit, habituation, and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: No definite boundary can be drawn between skill and habit; skill is generally the capacity of speedy habituation. Habit makes actions easy; habituation makes them necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction diagnostically: bodily skills (riding, swimming, skating, cycling) show habit and skill inseparable — actions done 'without thinking' are habitual. Recognize when an asserted ability might be habitual (automatic) rather than consciously skilled; this affects credibility of claims about noticing or performing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require tests or corroboration for asserted habits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a witness asserts that some action was habitual, test the assertion since without testing the possibility of error is still great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for demonstrable facts (examples: physician who counts pulse without a watch; merchant who estimates weight within a few grams). Where habit is alleged to explain otherwise inexplicable events, seek external confirmation — habits of isolated individuals are especially hard to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about inferring habit from isolated, odd anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits that explain unusual conduct often occur mainly in isolated people (old bachelors/old maids) and are difficult to establish because confirmation by others is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat surprising individual-habit testimony skeptically and demand corroboration; be aware many personally-known habits would be hard to prove in court despite being true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for 'refraction of thought' (habitual concurrence of speech and thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual concurrence of the real thought and what is said (refraction of an idea by the presence of another) frequently occurs and can correct or contradict spoken statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe each word carefully and compare speech to evident thought (e.g., slips like 'Unprepared, as I have--' or contradictory phrases revealing hidden admissions). These 'refractions' are diagnostic of exaggeration, evasion, or partial truth but require time and precise attention to detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on heredity to justify a 'congenital criminal' claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature on heredity cannot legitimately support the premise of a congenital criminal; particular properties may be inherited but great, essential changes that make a criminal are not directly inherited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Darwinian and heredity literature with caution; recognize inheritance of minor traits (features, interests, diseases, capacities), but avoid simplistic claims that a criminal's essential nature is inherited. The son of a criminal need not become a criminal; long-term selection across generations (rare) would be required to produce a 'criminal type.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Study heredity literature but apply it cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an enormous literature on heredity that every criminalist should study, but it tells us nothing definitive about criminality as a congenital trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of conflicting authorities (Darwin, Weismann, Lombroso, etc.) and of disputed claims (inheritance of acquired traits). Use hereditary explanations only as one possible background factor, not as determinative evidence of criminal responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively search for prepossession (prejudice, anticipatory opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepossession, prejudice, and anticipatory opinion are dangerous foes of the criminalist; they suffuse minds so that events can no longer be honestly observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a thoroughly careful search for any indication of prepossession; be alert to early-established views (first informer/witness advantage) and to the difficulty of reversing an initial accepted narrative. Train to set aside prejudices when their invalidity is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize sources and manifestations of prepossession
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepossession arises from egoism (projecting one's experiences), similar past cases, timing/first-information effects, names, behavior, pleasantnesses, and situational annoyances (examiner's mood/time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for one-sided apperception (seeing only what one already has in mind), influence of the first witness, favorable treatment or pleasant demeanor producing bias, and even trivial cues (a person's name) altering judgment. Where signs of prepossession exist, require extra effort to reconsider alternative views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for situational/transient prejudice in evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transient prejudices may arise from immediate circumstances (e.g., an inconvenient late complaint that strains patience) and are natural; they should be recognized, limited, and later corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that ephemeral prejudice will occur but ensure it remains transitive — calm and later handle the matter with scrupulous conscientiousness to repair any initial harm. Procedural safeguards or reexamination can mitigate these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imitation from duplication and investigate origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation (contagious copying) and duplication (independent recurrence) can both produce clusters of similar crimes or behaviors; their limits and contact points are often unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the origin of any stimulus or anticipatory image that might have led to imitation; among youth and women an anticipatory image often acts as a plan. Understanding whether an act arose from imitation may identify the likely perpetrator or motive. Acknowledge that epidemiologic/clinical duplication (e.g., disease patterns) may mimic imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess crowd dynamics and their especial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds often behave irrationally, dangerously, and criminally toward others under panic (e.g., stampedes, fires); the 'soul of the crowd' can produce excesses disconnected from individual responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating collective incidents, determine how much of the action is attributable to crowd contagion versus individual intent; note that calm individuals in crowds may do 'the silliest things' under moral contagion. Consider role of instigators (lunatics, drunkards) and the macro-psychology of mobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect against passion and affection bias (in examiner and witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion and affection cause confusion of observations, influence testimony, and can affect guilt; both examiners and witnesses are vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being overcome by passion; the best criminalists are lively but must control temperament. Do not quarrel with suspects/witnesses (a single improper word can ruin a case). For witnesses, expect exaggeration, emotion-driven falsehoods or amplification; for victims, reactions vary (extreme harm may produce calm rather than exaggeration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and interpret emotions like hatred, envy, and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred, envy, and fear have characteristic effects on testimony and behavior: envy is subtle and often detected by hesitation/reserved answering; fear has typical physical signs; passions may transmute into opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to hesitation and guarded responses as indicators of envy; observe physiological fear markers (irregular breathing, short breaths followed by deep ones, speech disturbances, pupil dilation, yawning) but remember innocent people may not show 'true' terror and emotions can invert (fear -> cold indifference). Use these cues cautiously and corroborate with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand 'honor' as a motive and as an investigative lever (but do not exploit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honor (one's sense of social standing) influences conduct even among criminals; thieves, burglars, and other offenders may have professional distinctions and a sense of honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize points at which a defendant seeks to preserve 'honor' (e.g., unwillingness to be associated with a particular class of crime). Such tendencies can be used as investigative clues in examination, but one must not exploit a suspect's pliability or dishonestably manipulate honor to elicit confessions or accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for superstition and consult specialized references when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition may influence behavior and testimony; the author refers to specialized works for its discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When superstition appears relevant, consult the cited references (Handbuch für Untersuchungsrichter; H. Gross's Archiv entries) for detailed treatment rather than relying on ad hoc assumptions.
